I see no reason not to use my own diagram for demonstration purposes. Instead, I'm being given a diagram which I do not believe is entirely accurate and which I therefore refuse to sign at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us what's inaccurate about this diagram, then.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- there is no open ground, open area, between the Studio C building and the passerelle walkway building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean it's not there? It's actually there in the diagram.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see one. Maybe it's there now, for all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. The walkway, the passerelle Building, and Studio C are not separated, two separate buildings; right? Okay. Give us your own diagram so that we can see your representation of the disposition of these buildings too. We can have that on the ELMO and keep this in e-court to compare the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By all means. It's your diagram, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The projectile came in under a small angle of descent. Our estimate at the time was about 25 degrees. It ricochetted off the roof here, it impacted on the vertical wall of the adjacent building, it again ricochetted and finally exploded on the ground right in front of the outside wall of the Studio C building. From the time it ricochetted and the time it impacted, several seconds went by. There were several witnesses who were standing relatively close to the scene of the incident. One person was killed on the spot. This person was standing in this area where the cars were parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zecevic, what about the angle of descent before the projectile ricochetted? Your call was about 25 degrees. And what about the angle when the projectile was on its way out?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I can't say that because no living person can possibly make that call.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, once it had ricochetted, the projectile went back up; right? That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we talk about rocket-assisted systems of this type, if there are three rocket engines involved, that is not necessarily the case. When we talk about artillery systems, yes, that would be the answer. As for rocket-assisted systems of this type, which I assumed had been used, the links between the warhead and the rocket engines are quite weak, so that is not necessarily the case. It all depends on the condition of the projectile as it came in and impacted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D3284 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, say you're playing with pebbles on a beach. You throw it, it ricochets, it hits the ground and goes back up. Otherwise you just dropped it into the water; right? That was the only way for it not to ricochet and go back up.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This projectile ricochetted at a very small angle and immediately hit the external wall of the building right opposite. We don't know the exact angle of impact. Was it lateral, was it frontal? We do know that it ended up towards the very bottom of that open ground between the two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at page 126 of your own document, sir. Look at the left-hand side marked by the yellow arrow. This is the spot that you believe the projectile to have landed on its bottom side, not its front side, so to speak, and it continued to -- on a horizontal trajectory. Or do you suppose that it would have bounced back up?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An air bomb, Mr. Karadzic, has a not-so-thin front end. What we see here, the red print on the ground, is the spot where the ogival part of the projectile impacted, not the fuse. The projectile simply slid along this small surface and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slid along the surface. Just a minute, please. Did it bounce back up?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It slid along the surface. And then if you look closely at this, you can see there is a small wall there, like a curb, so it bounced back up ever so site slightly, impacted on the vertical wall right opposite, bounced off the vertical wall which you can see in the following photograph, and then hit or landed at the far end of this open ground between the two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which part of the projectile hit the building opposite from there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The flat bottom of the projectile make the impact or the fuse?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that the explosion occurred at the far end of this open ground between the two buildings, right in front of the Studio C building wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the photograph on the right-hand side, the middle one - you have the two arrows there - do those two arrows mark the place of the second ricochet for this projectile?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that the projectile -- that the front end of the projectile, the fuse, impacted in that spot without the fuse igniting?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the type of system that was used, there was probably some sort of delay. When you have an air bomb, each and every fuse can have a delayed-action effect which can be adjusted, and this was probably used here. So this system can pierce through a building and then eventually explode inside a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would the damage be, considering the fact that the velocity was over a 500 kilometres per hour?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, at the time of impact against the roof, the system had already spent the best part of its force. The second time it impacted against the vertical wall, again it lost some of its force and energy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How much exactly? How would you estimate the loss?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a calculation which no man alive can make, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at what we have on the ELMO now. That's your own diagram, sir. You claim this projectile came in, but the diagram shows no angle of ascent, and you claim it bounced back up at a sharp angle, subsequently hitting the Studio C building wall; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The projectile came in, slid along with a very slight ricochet. We no longer know whether the trajectory was a regular one. At this point in time, the rocket engines must have broken off. We know that it impacted against the wall of the building across the way from there and we know that it ricochetted off the walkway building roof. That is a fact. But the facts also show, as far as the vertical walls of these buildings are concerned, that there were no shrapnel marks, no fragmentation marks, which would have been the case if a warhead like that had been used. All of the walls would have been pockmarked all over. 11.000 fragments or bits of shrapnel each way, 0.25 grams, or close to 7.000 bits of shrapnel, if you like, so these would be key data for you to make an estimate whether a projectile came in bearing a high-explosive warhead or a fuel-air warhead. These two different types. Nobody can deny that the projectile impacted against the TV building and eventually exploded on the ground just outside the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll be getting to that, which type of projectile, when, and how.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have D527. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again it's time to take a five-minute break now. --- Break taken at 11.52 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, on page 46, lines 22, 23, 24, 25, you said -- it's the transcript, today's transcript. You said that this projectile arrived, flew to this roof at an angle - beforehand you said a 25-degree angle - that it ricochetted, and that it had to bounce up and it did fly up and it impacted on that multi-storey building; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have -- actually, sorry, just one more clarification. When it approaches that building, the projectile rises; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you define what you mean by "rises"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It ascends?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So until the first ricochet, it descends. After that, it ascends towards the multi-storey building; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it is very simple. It is very simple to see where the projectile impacted from the moment of ricochet to the moment when it hit the vertical wall. You can see where the projectile impacted, and the angle can be determined. That's no problem. And that's not the point of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the point. Now, in order to impact this building, the multi-storey building, does it start descending again or does it continue to ascend?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in order to answer that question for you, we have to know whether the projectile maintained its structural integrity or not. If the projectile had not maintained its structural integrity or, rather, if the rocket engines were broken off, then its trajectory and its behaviour is unpredictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the rocket engines break off?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any information to the effect that rocket engines were found at the point of impact or explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the passerelle, the walkway building? Were they found anywhere within the TV compound?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The service that was in charge of this investigation did not provide me with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We do agree that that is about 300 kilograms, including the explosive and the engines and everything, at a speed of 540 kilometres per hour. Not more than 30 per cent can be lost at the first point of ricochet, so it continues at a speed of 300 kilometres per hour and it gets to the neighbouring building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D257 -- or actually 527, let's have a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, could I request that if the accused puts a series of assertions like that, including figures, to the witness, put them one by one to the witness to be sure that it does, in fact, agree to that, instead of moving straight on to his next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's even difficult for the Chamber to follow what the question is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that this projectile flew in at a speed of 150 metres per second, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You just put the question one by one to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you confirm today that this projectile, as it arrived, flew at a speed of 150 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that way. I said that the average cruising speed of the projectile was 150 to 180 metres per second, and that is a completely different figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D527 in e-court. Maybe something has been recorded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look at our diagram. Why don't you take a look at it. The projectile, when it first ricochetted, did it start ascending? That is what you confirmed then. Then it hit this building. Did it hit it while it was ascending or did it have to start descending again?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I told you, yet again, any hypothesis as to how the projectile ricochetted, how it behaved, depends significantly on its structural integrity, whether the rocket engines were on it or not. If the rocket engines are not there, there is not a single expert who is going to say how that projectile is going to behave, or predict what the trajectory will be. Anything can happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of physics?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physics is a law. Otherwise, I should not be a professor at the faculty of mechanical engineering. My entire integrity is based on natural laws that do not depend on man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well put. Now tell us: How did this projectile happen to be here, as if it were a dry leaf at a speed of a minimum of 300 kilometres per hour, provided that there were two ricochets at that? So how did that mass happen to be there at this kind of speed?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you look at my diagram, at the point of impact there is just one thing that I can establish. There was a ricochet off the flat surface of this passageway, and then the neighbouring vertical plane was hit, and then it ricochetted and fell on the ground, until the explosion there. And that is what I wrote in my study, and I provided my comment in relation to the effects of detonation; namely, that there were no fragments on vertical walls, that there is an intensive effect of the detonation waves on the vehicles that were in the immediate vicinity, and that these effects are mostly due to the fragments of sand and tiny particles -- well, I'm not an expert for this particular matter, but if you were to analyse the report of the man who was nearby and who later died in hospital, his blood vessels broke throughout his body due to the pressure that occurred there. And that is what I say in my statement, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you claim that all of that happened 10 metres, 15 metres, let it be 50 metres, as we had put it. Describe the trajectory of this projectile. How did it go from here to there? How did that happen and how did it hit the multi-storey building? Where are the rocket engines? What happened? Tell us. Was that established or do you have certain assumptions? Was it actually established what had happened?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, everything I had to say about this incident I said in my analysis. I repeated that before this Court. I said the same thing before the Trial Chamber in the proceedings against General Milosevic. And I have nothing to add to that. I cannot add anything to that. Everything else would be a hypothesis that is not scientifically supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this case, you claimed that a fuel-air bomb fell inter alia, because, as you said, the person who was a victim was practically without any clothing. That is what your February 1996 statement says; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, my technical report that I signed, together with two of my colleagues, in this case is my official report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 09997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement in February 1996?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the 65 ter number is 09997, page 1. And then we are going to move on to page 6 in English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the report -- or, rather, statement?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in English and Serbian, please. Page 4 from the top. I believe it's the same in English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The bottom part of page 4: "People from the TV building explained to me that the victim was naked after the explosion. This is typical of a blast effect. They could see blood flowing from his mouth, which indicated that he suffocated on his own blood, which is another typical sign. The other two witnesses were only three metres away from the point of explosion and they were temporarily deafened. They had shelter behind some pillar." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my statement, not my conclusion. I can draw a conclusion if I carry out an analysis. I just conveyed what people had said and I wrote that in my statement. A conclusion is a different matter. I believe that from a legal point of view there is a difference as well. From a technical point of view, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you accepted and included in your statement that you had been told that people survived only three metres from the explosion and only temporarily went deaf because they were sheltered by a pillar although it was an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just conveyed what people said here. But my technical report says whether I decided whether it was the effect of a fragmentation bomb or a fuel-air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fuel-air bomb; that is what my question should say. So you claim that it was a fuel-air bomb, although three metres away from the point of explosion two persons survived because they were protected by a pillar; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what is written here is the projectile exploded less than 10 metres away from that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The other two witnesses were only 3 metres away from the point of explosion and were temporarily deafened -- and temporarily went deaf; they had sheltered behind a pillar?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they stated, Mr. Karadzic. Not I. I just wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have a look at this. Did you conclude -- or, rather, what was your conclusion what fell in Tuzla at the gate? What kind of shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, does this have anything to do with my testimony here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It does. You'll see.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karadzic, but I was not addressing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. Mr. Karadzic, what do you mean by the shell that fell in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zecevic investigated the fall of a shell in Tuzla. I am going to show the effects of that shell now. Now I'm asking Mr. Zecevic what he concluded, what shell exploded in Tuzla, a fuel-air bomb, an air bomb, or a 130-millimetre shell, on the 25th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But could you let us know how that is related to this case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The effect of this shell was that since it was a fuel-air bomb, the man lost his clothing. I'm just asking you for a bit of patience, although I'm a lay person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What exploded in Tuzla? Was it a 130-millimetre bomb, a fuel-air bomb, or an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, at the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the case against General Djukic, I analysed the causes that led to the killing and wounding of many young people, and I assessed the zone from which it was possible for that projectile to arrive. On the basis of my analysis and the analysis of my colleagues who worked together with me, we established that at the location called Kapija, the gate, in Tuzla, there was an explosion of a 130-millimetre projectile that came from mount Ozren.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to get to that. General Djukic, an innocent man, was found guilty on account of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But now, let us have the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was 130 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of that unnecessary statement, the interpreter was not able to hear what you said. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellency, the gentleman, the witness, mentioned General Djukic in order to amplify the effect of his statement. And I am saying that that general was found guilty, although he is an innocent man. And we can find that there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was unnecessary. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, may I make a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, a statement in response to a statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, let's move on. Move on to your next topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this video from 1600. What we are going to show now is a recording from the location of that explosion of 130 millimetres at Kapija, the gate, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the victim remained without any clothing here?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D38 -- 3286. Can we see that photograph in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see now that this is a naked person?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, Mr. Karadzic. The resolution is exceptionally poor. It was on the 25th of May, warm weather. There is nothing I can say to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it remains that you were informed there at the TV station that 3 metres away from the explosion of the alleged fuel-air bomb people survived, though going deaf, because they were protected by a pillar. No other consequences; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm a very fair person. Everything that I, as a technical person, saw and heard, I recorded. As for my own thoughts, technically speaking, I conveyed that too. You are asking me about this and I am fully aware of the consequences of your question, if I can put it that way. But also, I was highly professional because I never wanted to embellish my reports or to shorten them in any way. I conveyed what people had said to me, and I have said to you several times now, an explosion happened, a concrete wall was destroyed. No one can say that an explosion had not taken place. No one can say that the destruction of the wall never happened. On the vertical walls, there are no fragments. The probable estimate is that this effect was caused by a fuel-air bomb. That is my statement and I stand by that statement. I'm not disassociating myself from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, why did you not disqualify this piece of information, that people survived although they were only 3 metres away from the point of explosion of a fuel-air bomb? And yesterday you said to us that that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it is in normal circumstances. However, in Sarajevo, I have witnesses, my neighbours, who were 7 metres away from the point of explosion of a 155-millimetre shell. That is statistically impossible but it is true. A 12-year girl was standing 7 metres away from the point of explosion and she survived. That is something that I as a professional also find totally amazing but it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, it wasn't a fuel-air bomb.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A weapon is a weapon, Mr. Karadzic. And very often the effects of weapons are based on statistics and statistical analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us leave theory aside. Let us stick with the bombs that we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I briefly have, once again, 1D3284.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is your statement or your report. While we are waiting for that, your conclusion is that since there are no fragments, damage of that kind, it had to be a fuel-air bomb rather than an air bomb; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the only two possible answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we take into account that there are no rocket engines there, is there a third option that is possible, that it is a shell of a different origin?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to define the calibre of the shell or projectile?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3284.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zecevic, let us see what it is that we can rule out. So if there are no rocket engines there, if there are no fragments there, if there is a great deal of destruction there, as we will see right now, on this wall, and if we see concrete breaking, is there any other possibility but a fuel-air bomb or an air bomb? And also, if victims survived although there were only -- they were only 3 metres away, is there a third, fourth, or fifth option that is also there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For your information, Mr. Karadzic, at the time when I was familiarising myself with the effects of this incident, I think it was two hours upon my arrival at the point of explosion, 100 metres away from the TV building, opposite the building of the geodesy institute, there was an explosion of yet another rocket-assisted projectile with an air bomb next to a container, a garbage container, and I think that the building is about 50 metres away from that point, and on that building, there were absolutely no fragments. There was a big hole, if I can put it that way, where rocket engines were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this. Can you see any fragments there, any traces?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in to these two bottom photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are there any traces of fragments there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are small fragments or, rather, effects of fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the reinforced concrete here? Was it broken?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also dealt with the incident in the street --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, actually, is it time for a break now, or should I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have spent half of the time allotted to you, so think about how to efficiently use your precious time. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 5 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we have to leave this segment for the time being, with the air bombs, and we are going to finish that tomorrow if we get a little bit more time, and some other elements of credibility. Now, let us start dealing with Markale 1 now. Is it correct that you volunteered to investigate the Markale incident of the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not volunteer to do the investigation. I volunteered to clarify and to give my opinion of what happened in Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you decided to do this when you heard the UNPROFOR commander say that it was not possible to determine the origin of the shell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that it was impossible to determine where the projectile came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did you hear that in the media?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, after the actual incident. Because I didn't have electricity at the time in order to be able to follow what was going on in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this was announced or published when?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are we going to then just leave this aside?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think the court reporter's having difficulty, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that have to do with us or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems that the LiveNote is working again. We can start again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 56, and can we actually add, I asked whether -- when we were defining the shell in Tuzla, I had said that it's not an aerosol bomb nor an air bomb, and this was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So let us just not deal with who the commander was. You said that you had heard General Smith but actually it was General Rose; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. How did you answer? It was not noted. The interpreters couldn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to be very precise in my answer. I heard the then-UNPROFOR commander saying that it was not possible to determine where the projectile came from. This is my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned this because in earlier statements Mr. Zecevic said that he had heard General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I accept that as an error and say it was General Rose. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was precise in my statement that the commander of the UNPROFOR stated. I don't want to discuss the names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Other than what you heard, did you have any other information from the local police or from other investigation teams at the time when you decided to get involved?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was not a favourite person of the local political power in Sarajevo at the time and am not now. I reported to my colleague who was the head of the criminal investigations unit. I knew him as my friend, and I suggested that I could help him in identifying the situation in Markale. So he called me to come the following day to that location. Nobody summoned me, and my influence in Sarajevo at that time, and even later, is insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You concluded from somewhere that you would be able to correct this statement that was made, that it was not possible to determine where the shell came from; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was clear. I felt that it was possible to assess the direction from where the shell came from. And this is a method that has been in use in military technology for quite some years now, the determination where -- from which direction the projectile comes from, if there are clear indications at the scene of the explosion. So it's not something that is up to me. It's not something that I made up or devised. This is something that comports with the already existing rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, in your apartment you heard UNPROFOR saying that it was not possible to determine where the shell came from, but you said it can be determined. So based on what did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for a reference for these assertions, please, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three or four lines on this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I don't have anything on my monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page, Mr. Karadzic, you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the previous page, if this is page 2, Mr. Zecevic said this was possible to do, and this is why I'm asking this. [In English] "I felt that it was possible to assess the direction from where the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, let's upload that document. What document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about today's transcript. He said, on page 2, line 12 onwards, that he felt that it was possible to determine this. This was his reaction to the UNPROFOR commander's statement that it was not possible to determine the direction of the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 2 covers Mr. Gaynor's submission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My page 2 has my question: [In English] "You concluded from somewhere that you would be able to correct this statement that was made, that it was not possible to determine where the shell came from; isn't that right?" [Interpretation] The answer is: [In English] "I think that I was clear. I felt that it was possible to assess the direction from where the shell came from." [Interpretation] This is page 2, line 12 onwards. Or we don't have the same transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're correct. When the LiveNote restarted, it started with page 1 again. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained that there are clear methods --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait, please. What made you think that you could do this better than the police and better than the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I had 17 years of experience of working in the military industry behind me. I was an extremely interested engineer in fragmentation effects and the effect of warheads on targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What expertise is this?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't need a lecture, Mr. Zecevic. Please answer my question. You concluded that you can do what they cannot do. What expertise was this that you did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt the witness in the middle of his answer. Please hear him out. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I offered my assistance in order that the direction of the incoming projectile could be determined. I offered this help to my colleague who was head of the criminal investigations unit because I felt that based on 17 years of prior work and studies in ammunition design and terminal ballistics, I could be useful there. This is quite a normal reaction of just an ordinary man in a town that was surrounded. I don't know why I should be ashamed of what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm not discussing any kind of shame here. I just want to establish what made you believe that you could determine this better than the UNPROFOR or the local police could?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want a detailed answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't need a detailed answer. Just tell me what led you to believe that you could do this job better.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police is not qualified to analyse the effects of military devices on targets. This is number 1. Number 2, UNPROFOR, these are the soldiers who use those devices, whose task it is to kill, not to analyse the effect and actions upon a target. This is something that is done by professionals, not soldiers. Soldiers are qualified to use those devices in order to kill the enemy. Therefore, I was qualified at that point in time to help the investigation organs of my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, the effects and the action upon the targets was not something that was in dispute. What was in dispute was the incoming -- the direction of the incoming shell and the place that it was fired from. Are you an expert in establishing the distance from the -- which the shell was fired and the direction of the incoming shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, up until that time, how many studies or analyses did you carry out in order to establish the place of firing and the distance from which the shell was fired?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, that was my first attempt to work for a civilian institution. Before that, I had thousands of fired rocket and artillery projectiles and hundreds of fired warheads in testing ranges behind me. So up until that time, I was an exceptionally qualified person to study the effects of fired projectiles upon targets. I can also say that in peacetime there is no need to analyse the effects of weapons on civilian targets. It was not necessary for me to do things like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D3114, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that we can see how many projectiles or shells you had actually fired. And while we are waiting, Mr. Zecevic, we are not talking about the effects here. What was disputed here was the origin of the shell. You did not agree with the conclusion of the UNPROFOR commander and you believed that you could do this, and this is why you volunteered. That was your goal. Not to evaluate the effects of the actual projectile.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's impossible to establish the incoming characteristics without studying the effects on the target. First of all you have to have the fragmentation effects on the target. And once you determine that, then you can talk about deciphering the direction from where the shell came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please pay attention to this document now. Have you heard of this technical testing centre?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they answer here to our inquiry that: "Further to your request for the provision of information on the engagement of Berko Zecevic at the technical training centre, from 1976 to 1992." You can see that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In [indiscernible] the table below represents the details held in the archives. Can you please tell us how much of what did you fire? And we can see that on this table.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1977, 18 rockets, then four rockets, on the 7th of January -- February, 1977. Then in 1985. Then in 1984, 199. Then from the 2nd of October to the 23rd of October, 101. Then on the 9th of November to the 20th of November, 14. On the 28th of January, 1986, three. Then on the 6th of February, 1986, 21. Then on the 6th of May, 1986, 14. Then on the 3rd of October to the 24th of October, 1986, 102. Then on the 28th of October 1986, 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, all right. Well, that is sufficient. We can see that. Mr. Zecevic, throughout your whole career you fired less than 1.000 overall, and 120 mines, only five. This is contained in line 2.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you did not provide any studies where you would be required to determine the direction and the distance that a mortar mine would cover.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is never done in peacetime. This is only done in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1093, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive at the place of the incident? This was on the 6th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you at the scene on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you please remind me, the massacre occurred on the 5th. I got there at 8.00 in the morning on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interrupt. At the start of this portion of the cross-examination, Dr. Karadzic referred to this incident taking place on the 5th. It took place on the 4th of February. Now, I don't want him to embed that misunderstanding into further questions. The incident took place on the 4th of February. If we can work from there, please. I don't think that's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is quite a disputable thing. What is not in dispute is that it occurred on the 5th. Dobrinja occurred on the 4th. However, perhaps the witness needs a break. We'll always agree. It's not necessary for anyone to jump in to save him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, I don't need anyone to jump in and save me. I was crystal clear on this. The day the massacre occurred, that evening I phone my colleague. And the next day, at 8.00 in the morning I appeared at the scene. We conducted an analysis and that took about 36 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, you agree that it took place on 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll have to come back to you. Our indictment has the 4th of February. I'll have to come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's G 8, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. My apologies to the Court and to Mr. Karadzic. My mistake. It was the 5th of February. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need to lose any sleep over this because this is the smallest of your mistakes. The other mistakes that you have made are of much greater significance, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's time to have another break. We will break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 1.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small intervention in the transcript, please. I said this is the smallest mistake in the indictment, and not Mr. Gaynor's specifically. I said all the other mistakes in the indictment are greater. It wasn't a personal remark at the expense of Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You phoned someone that evening, but who did you speak to when you arrived at the scene?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An acquaintance of mine who was the head of the technical department of the crime squad at the time. He introduced me to the investigating magistrate who was there whose name now escapes me. Another three of my colleagues arrived with me. Two of them worked in the Pretis factory and the third worked in the UNIS institute. Before that he used to work in the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory producing plastic explosives. The magistrate believed that he could use our help. He appointed us as members of a committee charged with establishing what exactly had occurred at Markale back in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you appeared in the Milosevic trial --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 1D3316 for everyone's reference, page 35 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- you said you reported to this magistrate, you introduced yourself, and he appointed you as a member of that committee. Did you receive your appointment in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The e-court reference is page 55. That's 1D3316, page 55.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I received a decision in writing on that very day or the next day. I'm unsure about which day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that decision available for us to see?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me? I -- it is certainly not my duty to carry it on me or to bring it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber agrees then that's fine, but it certainly might be helpful to us if we had that.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can suspend the trial and my appearance here. I could travel back to Sarajevo and bring a copy here or perhaps submit a copy additionally. Should the Chamber so require, you can have a copy ordered from the original court that issued the decision. That can be forward directly to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It reads: The magistrate was there, I introduced myself, I had two of my colleagues over there who were ballistic experts, and another colleague, and the three of us were appointed by the magistrate as experts who were supposed to provide an expert opinion. The question is: Who to?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the magistrate. Because he was the person who appointed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were there in what official capacity exactly? Were you investigators or experts?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were committee members, panel members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who headed the panel or the committee?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I was the most senior person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the magistrate proceed to suspend the previous investigation team then?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me. It's not part of my remit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly put a pause. Just wait a bit and start answering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the magistrate have an investigation team from the police and another team, and that was your team?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not privy to the working procedures that they used at the time. All I know is the magistrate set up this panel and we were given some work to do, which we did. The police were there to make certain photographs available to us, which they did. And they also provided any -- any spare parts that were found on the scene, following our arrival at Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it not true the magistrate asked you to get everything done and dusted within a 36-hour deadline?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly asked us to get on with it and be as quick as we could. The general atmosphere that prevailed in Sarajevo at the time was such that we were expected to deal with this in the shortest possible order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about your findings, your conclusions? Did that become part of the investigative material collected by the magistrate?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question for you. My colleagues and I put together a report, we signed it off, and we submitted it to the magistrate. I don't know what became of it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You quoted two persons there, Ahmed Hadziomerovic and Amir Kurtovic. Hadziomerovic is the officer and there was Kurtovic, Amir. Who was the third person?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zijo Pekic. He was a ballistics expert. He completed a specialised course back in Belgrade. Hadziomerovic was a professional officer of the JNA, a Major by rank. He completed his education at the military technical school in Zagreb, and then he followed a specialised course of study later on, also in Zagreb. He was an exceptionally competent professional and a distinguished expert. Amir Kurtovic was a professional officer dealing with explosives, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There's no need to have this page of the transcript admitted. It has been confirmed already. Did you enlist the assistance of any ethnic Serbs when you started work as a panel?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that is not where I draw my distinction. Not along ethnic lines. At the time, those persons were my closest associates and they also happened to be the closest in terms of their geographical location. They were neighbours. Do not insinuate that I displayed any form of nationalism whatsoever in my behaviour. I do not discriminate along ethnic or religious lines. I never have. I never will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Dobrljo [phoen] Stanic, who took a specialised study course in France, what about Radisav Markovic, your other colleagues from the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were my friends, and, as a matter of fact, remain my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it a series of ethnic clashes that we were looking at, at the time, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you mean, Sarajevo or Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I certainly do not believe that these were ethnic clashes or an ethnic conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why was it not an ethnic conflict? What was it then? Was it a class-based conflict? Was it a religion-based conflict?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it has been 17 or 18 years since 1992 and I'm still wondering why it happened. I still can't explain this to myself. Why did we start killing each other over something that was not a spiritual matter but, rather, purely material?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it possible that Serbs were involved in the work of this committee?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly not communicated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your panel conducted this investigation on the 6th of February, 1994, the day after the incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the place of the incident? On the 6th of February, when you started your investigation, had it already been cleared and substantially altered, the scene?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Beforehand, members of the Security Services Centre from Sarajevo had carried out an on-site investigation and there was also a succession of UNPROFOR teams investigating the scene of the incident. You did not gain access to any findings by the Security Services Centre before you started your own examination of the site?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their findings had not been available to me -- had not been made available to me yet, but I did have access to the photographs that were taken and to the tail fins that were found at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you some footage, a recording, a video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1D1031. The range is between 11.10 and 11.26.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this man with the glasses?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is this?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the manager of the UNIS institute, the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's his profession?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a Ph.D. in electronics, electrical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in electrical engineering?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. The memories I hold of that person are not particularly fond. Quite the contrary, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Faruk Orucevic; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree about the surname, Orucevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Faruk Orucevic Ejup Ganic's successor as head of the institute?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure he was Ejup Ganic's successor, but he became head of the institute right after Ganic left. I do know that I received orders from the BH army to go and work at the UNIS institute. Otherwise I would be tried. I would be facing charges. Orucevic was head of the UNIS institute at the time I worked there. That much I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Mr. Orucevic now? Is he not a professor and associate at Ejup Ganic's private university?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I do not privately socialise with either of these two persons, Ejup Ganic or indeed Orucevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So Faruk Orucevic, a BA in electrical engineering, what was his capacity as a member of this team that conducted an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he did not take part in this investigation. He was present there, he was my boss. I needed a computer and a printer to use in my work, and he was the only one who actually had both pieces of equipment back in his office. When I headed out with my associates, we were on our way to the scene of the incident and we wanted to check something else and he asked to come along. I said I had no authority to take him there. But he just turned up, he introduced himself, he was just there. He was a by-stander. He was not part of the investigation. He did not sign the report. But apparently he liked to show his face around and show himself off as an important person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But he did make a statement to the media, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, I'm sorry, can this be admitted, please? We have another one with the same number, so perhaps we could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another one. So we can have a single number for both or two different numbers. And we can run the other one now. Thank you. 13.51 until 14.04. That's the range.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We didn't hear the sound. That's Mr. Orucevic; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we headed out, then we left the Markale square. I banned all members of my panel from making any public statements and pronouncements. I realised that there were TV crews standing around recording. Orucevic was there when I said that no one would be allowed to make any statements to the press. He realised, if he watched the footage, that I simply walked past them with my colleague. Nevertheless, he likes to be very much in the public eye. He made a colossal error there. He made an unauthorised statement to the press.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please run the tape again. I hope that the sound is clear enough for our interpreters to try and see if they can figure out what the people in the tape are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll need to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit these two clips. I was told that this is part -- another part of this clip has been marked for identification as D894. But setting that aside, we will admit these two clips.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, following your investigation, the investigation carried out by your panel, you drew up a report in which item 9 reads -- perhaps you'd like me to call the document up; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Today we don't have that luxury. We have to get out of this room as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, you should please consider giving me more time tomorrow, because we have not even touched upon a number of substantial incidents, and we have no other witnesses coming whose presence we can use to shed light on these.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, we have to get out of this room. Tomorrow, 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of February, 2011, at 1.30 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
